newsitem.title: UK: Pearson's Scardino must win over sceptics.
newsitem.headline: Pearson's Scardino must win over sceptics.

text.p: Marjorie Scardino faces a tough battle to win over sceptics when she becomes chief executive of British media group Pearson at the end of the year.

Selecting an American woman to head a top British company was certain to raise a few eyebrows in the City of London. But initial doubts are paradoxically based on the fact that she is seen as a Pearson insider rather than a new broom.
"The message that this appointment puts across is that we can expect more of the same from the company. That's not what the market wanted to hear," said one media analyst.
A lawyer before moving into media management, Scardino, 49, is a relative unknown to most analysts and that is another factor behind the cool initial response to her appointment.

Pearson shares slid 11 1/2p to 676 1/2p after the company, whose interests range from Australian soap opera to the Financial Times newspaper, ended long speculation over who would succeed Frank Barlow when he retires at the end of the year.

Scardino is chief executive of The Economist Newspaper Ltd, 50 percent owned by Pearson. The group, which publishes a number of business titles including The Economist magazine, has more than doubled its profits in her three years in charge.
She is also on the board of ConAgra Inc, a U.S. food company based in Nebraska but share analysts questioned whether she had the experience required to run Pearson.

"The market was looking for an outside appointment, someone with a big company track record. She's apparently been very successful at the Economist but it's not the same as running a major PLc," said one City analyst.
Pearson has sold off businesses in wine, china and oil services in recent years to focus on three media-related areas -- Information, Education and Entertainment.
But its critics say that it lacks focus and it has long been seen as a prime candidate for takeover by one of its rivals in the media or leisure sectors.
The appointment of Scardino is seen as confirmation of Pearson's commitment to its Information businesses, which include newspaper interests in France and Spain.
Born in Arizona, Scardino worked in the 1970s as a lawyer in Savannah, Georgia -- the hometown of her journalist husband.
By night she helped him work on his weekly Georgia Gazette newspaper, a title that won a Pulitzer prize for its investigative reporting but ultimately failed to make money.
She moved to New York in the mid 1980s where she headed the Economist's North American operations for several years.
She lives in the swish west London quarter of Knightsbridge with husband Albert. The couple have three children -- one of whom is making a name for himself as an actor.

Indeed, Hal Scardino, 11, is maybe better known than his high-powered Mum. His films include Marvin's Room with Meryl Streep, Diane Keaton and Robert de Niro and The Indian in the Cupboard, for which he won a best child actor award.
